observation_summary: The DateUtils.truncate method incorrectly handles Daylight Saving Time (DST) transitions because it relies on Calendar.set(), which triggers side effects (like resetting DST offsets) even when the field value remains unchanged. This causes the truncated date to shift by an hour.
hypothesis: The original implementation relied on Calendar.set() to perform truncation, which is side-effect prone during DST transitions. The fix replaces this approach with manual time arithmetic on the underlying long timestamp, avoiding unnecessary Calendar state updates.
prediction: The code will move away from using Calendar.set() for lower-level time fields (milliseconds, seconds, minutes) and instead perform direct arithmetic on the time value, only updating the Calendar object when a change is actually required.
experiment_rationale: The diff shows a complete rewrite of the truncation logic for milliseconds, seconds, and minutes, replacing Calendar.set() calls with direct long-based arithmetic and a conditional update to the Calendar object. This confirms the procedural logic was flawed for the specific domain of time manipulation.
reasoning_summary: The defect is an incorrect computational strategy for truncating time fields. While the fix includes a guard (if offset != 0), the primary mechanism of the fix is a complete rewrite of the truncation algorithm to avoid the side effects of the Calendar API, which is a classic Algorithm/Method defect.
evidence_used: The diff shows a complete rewrite of the truncation logic for milliseconds, seconds, and minutes.
The fix replaces Calendar.set() calls with direct long-based arithmetic.
The bug report explicitly mentions that Calendar.set() resets fields like DST_OFFSET even when the value is unchanged.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix adds a check (if offset != 0), the core issue is the reliance on an incorrect computational approach (Calendar.set) for time truncation, which required a procedural rewrite.
This is a local procedural issue within the DateUtils class, not a missing design-level capability.
